notes.definition: Efficiency is the proportion of the total input energy (or power) that is transferred usefully: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer.
explanation: The energy efficiency of any energy transfer can be calculated with efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer. Because power is the rate of energy transfer, efficiency can also be calculated as efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input. You must recall both forms. Efficiency has no units: it is a ratio of two energies (or two powers), so it is written as a decimal (such as 0.25) or as a percentage (25%) by multiplying the decimal by 100.

No real device is 100% efficient. In every energy transfer some energy is dissipated, usually by heating the device and its surroundings, or as sound. Energy is conserved, so the total input energy = useful output energy + wasted energy. This means efficiency can never be greater than 1 (100%); a calculated value above 1 shows a mistake, such as dividing the wrong way round.

You need to rearrange the efficiency equation confidently. Useful output = efficiency × total input, and total input = useful output ÷ efficiency. If a question gives a percentage, convert it to a decimal (divide by 100) before using it in the equation. Make sure both energies are in the same units, for example both in J (not one in kJ), and if you are given power and time, calculate energy using E = P × t with time in seconds.

Higher tier students should be able to describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer. The general idea is to reduce the energy that is dissipated. Lubricating moving parts reduces friction; thermal insulation reduces unwanted energy transfer by heating; using wires or components with lower resistance reduces electrical heating; streamlining reduces air resistance; and tightening loose parts reduces vibration and sound. Replacing a filament lamp with an LED is a common example: the LED transfers far less energy to the thermal store of the surroundings for the same light output.

Diagrams called Sankey diagrams are often used to show efficiency. The width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy, with the useful output going straight on and the wasted energy bending away. Reading values from these diagrams lets you calculate efficiency quickly.
keyFacts: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer (recall).
efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input (recall).
Efficiency has no units; it can be a decimal or a percentage (× 100).
No device is 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated.
Total input energy = useful output energy + wasted energy.
Efficiency can never be greater than 1 (100%).
Rearranged: useful output = efficiency × total input; total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.
Convert a percentage to a decimal (÷ 100) before using it in a calculation.
(HT) Efficiency is increased by reducing wasted energy: lubrication, insulation, lower resistance, streamlining.

keyTerms.definition: The proportion of total input energy or power that is transferred usefully.
The energy transferred to the store you want, such as light from a lamp or kinetic energy from a motor.
All the energy supplied to a device.
Energy that is dissipated to stores that are not useful, usually thermal stores of the surroundings.
A diagram where arrow widths are proportional to the energy transferred, showing useful and wasted energy.
The rate at which energy is supplied to a device, in watts.

equations.name: Efficiency (energy)
equations.formula: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer
equations.units: both energies in the same unit, usually joules (J); efficiency has no unit (decimal or %)

equations.name: Efficiency (power)
equations.formula: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
equations.units: both powers in the same unit, usually watts (W); efficiency has no unit (decimal or %)

workedExamples.title: Efficiency from energies
workedExamples.question: A lamp is supplied with 200 J of energy and gives out 50 J of light. Calculate its efficiency as a decimal and as a percentage.
steps: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy.

workedExamples.title: Efficiency from powers with kW
workedExamples.question: A motor has an input power of 1.5 kW and a useful power output of 1200 W. Calculate its efficiency.
steps: Convert to the same unit: 1.5 kW = 1500 W.
efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input = 1200 ÷ 1500.

workedExamples.title: Rearranging to find the input energy
workedExamples.question: A kettle is 85% efficient. It must transfer 340 kJ of energy to the water. Calculate the total input energy in kJ.
steps: Convert the percentage to a decimal: 85% = 0.85.
Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

workedExamples.title: Using power and time in minutes
workedExamples.question: A motor with an input power of 250 W runs for 2.0 minutes. It transfers 18 kJ of useful energy. Calculate its efficiency.
steps: Convert: t = 2.0 × 60 = 120 s; useful energy = 18 000 J.
Total input energy = P × t = 250 × 120 = 30 000 J.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often divide total input by useful output, getting an efficiency greater than 1.
misconceptions.right: In fact efficiency = useful output ÷ total input, so it is always less than 1 (less than 100%).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often give efficiency a unit such as J or W.
misconceptions.right: In fact efficiency is a ratio of two energies or two powers, so it has no unit.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a more powerful device is more efficient.
misconceptions.right: In fact power is the rate of energy transfer; efficiency is the fraction that is useful. A high-power device can be very inefficient.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think wasted energy is destroyed.
misconceptions.right: In fact wasted energy is dissipated, usually to the thermal store of the surroundings; total energy is conserved.

realWorld: Energy labels on fridges and washing machines rate appliances by how efficiently they use energy, helping buyers reduce bills.
Replacing filament lamps with LEDs greatly increases lighting efficiency, so far less electrical energy is wasted heating rooms.
Power stations recover some wasted thermal energy in combined heat and power schemes, using it to heat nearby homes.
higherTier: Describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer: reduce friction by lubrication, reduce unwanted heating with thermal insulation, use lower resistance wires and components to reduce electrical heating, streamline vehicles to reduce air resistance, and tighten or cushion parts to reduce vibration and sound.
Explain that each method increases efficiency because it reduces the energy dissipated, so a greater proportion of the input energy is transferred usefully.
examTips: Learn both forms of the efficiency equation; they are not on the equation sheet.
Check your answer: an efficiency above 1 or above 100% means you divided the wrong way.
Only give a % sign if you multiplied by 100; 0.6 and 60% are both correct, but 0.6% is wrong.
Make sure both energies (or both powers) are in the same unit before dividing.
For 'describe how to increase efficiency' questions, always say what wasted transfer is reduced and how.
summary: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (energy or power).
Efficiency has no units: decimal or percentage.
No device is 100% efficient; some energy is always dissipated.
Total input = useful output + wasted energy.
Rearrange to find input or useful output; convert % to a decimal first.
(HT) Increase efficiency by reducing wasted energy transfers.

questions.question: Which equation links efficiency, total input energy transfer and useful output energy transfer?
options: efficiency = total input energy ÷ useful output energy
efficiency = useful output energy × total input energy
efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy
efficiency = total input energy − useful output energy
markScheme: 1 mark: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy
questions.explanation: Efficiency is the fraction of the input that is useful, so useful output goes on top. Dividing the other way gives a value above 1, which is impossible. Subtracting gives the wasted energy.

questions.question:
A device has an efficiency of 0.65.
What is the efficiency of the device as a percentage?
markScheme: 1 mark: 65%
questions.explanation: Multiply the decimal by 100: 0.65 × 100 = 65%.

questions.question: What is the unit of efficiency?
options: joule (J)
watt (W)
joule per second (J/s)
It has no unit
markScheme: 1 mark: It has no unit
questions.explanation: Efficiency is energy ÷ energy (or power ÷ power), so the units cancel. It is a pure number or percentage.

questions.question: Which statement explains why the efficiency of a device can never be greater than 100%?
options: Devices always get hot
Energy cannot be created, so the useful output cannot be more than the input
Efficiency is measured in joules
The input power is always greater than 100 W
markScheme: 1 mark: Energy cannot be created, so the useful output cannot be more than the input
questions.explanation: By conservation of energy, useful output plus wasted energy equals input, so useful output is at most equal to input.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the total input energy and the useful output energy for four devices, A, B, C and D.
Which device is the most efficient?
options: A
B
C
D
markScheme: 1 mark: C
questions.explanation: Efficiencies: A = 0.50, B = 0.60, C = 0.75 and D = 0.45. Device D has the largest useful output (450 J) but is the least efficient; what matters is the fraction of the input that is useful.

questions.question:
A device has an efficiency of 30%. The total input energy is 600 J.
How much energy is wasted by the device?
markScheme: 1 mark: 420 J
questions.explanation: Useful output = 0.30 × 600 = 180 J, so wasted = 600 − 180 = 420 J. 180 J is the useful energy, not the wasted energy.

questions.question: Which change would increase the efficiency of an electric motor?
options: Increasing the input power
Lubricating the bearings to reduce friction
Running the motor for a longer time
Using thinner wires with a higher resistance
markScheme: 1 mark: Lubricating the bearings to reduce friction
questions.explanation: Lubrication reduces energy dissipated by friction, so a larger fraction of the input is useful. More power or longer running does not change the fraction; higher resistance wires waste more energy by heating.

questions.question:
A gas-fired power station has an efficiency of 35%.
Which statement about the power station is correct?
options: 35% of the energy is destroyed
65% of the input energy is transferred as electricity
The power station creates 35% more energy than it uses
65% of the input energy is dissipated, mostly to the thermal store of the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: 65% of the input energy is dissipated, mostly to the thermal store of the surroundings
questions.explanation: 35% is transferred usefully as electricity; the remaining 65% is wasted, much of it heating the surroundings via the cooling towers. Energy is never destroyed or created.

questions.question: Which change would increase the efficiency of an electric kettle the most?
options: Surrounding the kettle body with a layer of thermal insulation
Using a metal body with a higher thermal conductivity
Leaving the lid open while it boils
Using a heating element with a higher power
markScheme: 1 mark: Surrounding the kettle body with a layer of thermal insulation
questions.explanation: Insulation reduces energy transferred from the water and kettle to the surroundings, so more of the input goes into the water. A metal body or open lid increases losses; higher power heats faster but does not by itself change the fraction wasted.

questions.question:
An LED lamp and a filament lamp give out the same amount of light.
Why is the LED lamp more efficient?
options: It has a higher power input
It wastes less energy heating the surroundings
It transfers more energy as light per second than it takes in
It does not need electricity
markScheme: 1 mark: It wastes less energy heating the surroundings
questions.explanation: For the same useful light output, the LED needs a smaller input because less energy is dissipated as thermal energy. No lamp can give out more energy than it takes in.

questions.question:
The total input energy to a device is 100 J. The useful output energy is 30 J.
Calculate the efficiency of the device.
Give your answer as a decimal.
markScheme: 1 mark: efficiency = 30 ÷ 100
1 mark: 0.30
questions.explanation: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 30 ÷ 100 = 0.30 (equivalent to 30%).

questions.question:
The total input energy to a pulley system is 400 J. The useful output energy is 300 J.
Calculate the percentage efficiency of the pulley system.
markScheme: 1 mark: 75%
questions.explanation: 0.75 × 100 = 75%. The remaining 100 J is dissipated, mainly by friction in the pulleys.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a Sankey diagram for a television.
Calculate the percentage efficiency of the television.

markScheme: 1 mark: 70%
questions.explanation: Use the power form: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input = 84 ÷ 120 = 0.70 = 70%.

questions.question:
The total input energy to a motor is 2.5 kJ. The motor does 2000 J of useful work.
Calculate the percentage efficiency of the motor.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2.5 kJ = 2500 J
1 mark: 80%
questions.explanation: Convert to the same unit first. Dividing 2000 by 2.5 gives 800, an impossible efficiency, which shows the units were not matched.

questions.question:
A device has an efficiency of 40%. The total input energy is 1500 J.
Calculate the useful output energy of the device.
markScheme: 1 mark: useful output = 0.40 × 1500
1 mark: 600 J
questions.explanation: Convert 40% to 0.40 and rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.40 × 1500 = 600 J.

questions.question:
An LED lamp has an efficiency of 40%. The useful power output of the lamp is 12 W.
Calculate the total power input to the lamp.
markScheme: 1 mark: efficiency = 0.40
1 mark: total input = 12 ÷ 0.40
1 mark: 30 W
questions.explanation: Rearrange: total power input = useful power output ÷ efficiency = 12 ÷ 0.40 = 30 W. Multiplying instead gives 4.8 W, which is less than the output and therefore impossible.

questions.question:
A kettle has a power of 2.0 kW. The kettle is switched on for 3.0 minutes. The efficiency of the kettle is 90%.
Calculate the energy wasted by the kettle.
Give your answer in kilojoules.
markScheme: 1 mark: t = 180 s
1 mark: total input = 2000 × 180 = 360 000 J
1 mark: useful = 0.90 × 360 000 = 324 000 J (or wasted fraction = 0.10)
1 mark: wasted = 36 000 J = 36 kJ
questions.explanation: Input energy = P × t = 360 kJ. 90% is useful, so 10% is wasted: 0.10 × 360 = 36 kJ.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows an electric winch lifting a load.
The total input energy to the winch is 2.5 kJ. The winch lifts a 50 kg load through a height of 4.0 m.
Calculate the percentage efficiency of the winch.
Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

markScheme: 1 mark: useful output = mgh = 50 × 9.8 × 4.0 = 1960 J
1 mark: input = 2500 J
1 mark: 78%
questions.explanation: The useful output is the gain in gravitational potential energy, 1960 J. Efficiency = 1960 ÷ 2500 = 0.784, which is 78% to 2 s.f.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a Sankey diagram for a filament lamp.
The efficiency of the lamp is 5%.
Calculate the power wasted by the lamp.

markScheme: 1 mark: useful power = 0.05 × 60 = 3 W (or wasted fraction 0.95)
1 mark: wasted power = 57 W
questions.explanation: Only 5% (3 W) is useful light, so 60 − 3 = 57 W is wasted heating the surroundings.

questions.question: Write down the equation that links efficiency, useful output energy transfer and total input energy transfer.
acceptedAnswers: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer
markScheme: 1 mark: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer
questions.explanation: This must be recalled. The useful output is always on the top.

questions.question: Write down the equation that links efficiency, useful power output and total power input.
acceptedAnswers: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
efficiency = useful power out ÷ total power in
markScheme: 1 mark: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
questions.explanation: The power form is used when you are given powers in watts rather than energies in joules.

questions.question:
A machine has an efficiency of 0.25.
What percentage of the total input energy is wasted?
markScheme: 1 mark: 75%
questions.explanation: 0.25 = 25% useful, so 100 − 25 = 75% is wasted.

questions.question: Explain why no real device can be 100% efficient.
acceptedAnswers: energy transferred to thermal store of surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: in every energy transfer some energy is dissipated (wasted)
1 mark: for example by heating due to friction or electrical resistance, or as sound, so the useful output is less than the input
questions.explanation: There is always some unwanted transfer, usually heating, so useful output is always less than total input.

questions.question: An advert claims a new motor is 120% efficient. Explain why this claim must be false.
markScheme: 1 mark: 120% would mean the useful output is greater than the input
1 mark: energy cannot be created (conservation of energy), so efficiency cannot exceed 100%
questions.explanation: Since total input = useful output + wasted, the useful output can never exceed the input.

questions.question: An LED lamp and a filament lamp give out the same amount of light. Explain why the LED lamp is cheaper to run.
acceptedAnswers: less energy input needed for same light
markScheme: 1 mark: the LED is more efficient, wasting less energy heating the surroundings
1 mark: so it needs a smaller input power (less energy from the supply) for the same light, so it costs less
questions.explanation: Same useful output with higher efficiency means less total input energy, and you pay for input energy.

questions.question: Give two ways of increasing the efficiency of a car.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: lubricate moving parts to reduce friction; streamline the body to reduce air resistance; insulate the engine to reduce unwanted heating; tighten loose parts to reduce vibration and sound
questions.explanation: Each method reduces the energy dissipated, so more of the chemical energy from the fuel ends up in the kinetic store.

questions.question:
Thermal insulation is added around the body of an electric kettle.
Explain how this increases the efficiency of the kettle.
acceptedAnswers: more energy goes into the water
lower rate of energy transfer by heating
markScheme: 1 mark: insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating from the kettle and water to the surroundings
1 mark: so less energy is wasted (dissipated)
1 mark: so a greater proportion of the input energy goes into the thermal store of the water, increasing efficiency
questions.explanation: The useful output is the energy in the water. Reducing losses means more of the same input is useful, so useful output ÷ total input rises.

questions.question:
An engineer wants to increase the efficiency of the electric motor that drives a lift.
Describe the changes the engineer could make.
Explain how each change increases the efficiency.
markScheme: Indicative content: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input, so reducing wasted energy increases efficiency; lubricate the bearings and moving parts to reduce friction so less energy is dissipated by heating; use thicker copper wires (lower resistance) in the motor and cables so less energy is dissipated by electrical heating; reduce vibration by tightening or balancing parts so less energy is wasted as sound; use a counterweight so less energy is needed to lift the lift car; streamline or reduce air resistance in the lift shaft; regular maintenance to keep parts clean and aligned; total energy is conserved, so energy saved from waste becomes useful output or reduces input needed.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): at least three relevant changes, each linked clearly to the specific wasted energy transfer it reduces and to efficiency.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): two relevant changes with some explanation of how they reduce wasted energy.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two changes stated with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Every improvement works the same way: it cuts a wasted energy transfer (friction, electrical heating, sound), so a larger share of the input is useful.

questions.question:
Two kettles, A and B, each transfer 336 kJ of energy to the water inside them.
Table 1 shows the power of each kettle and the time each kettle takes.
Calculate the efficiency of each kettle.
Determine which kettle is more efficient.
markScheme: Indicative content: Kettle A: t = 210 s, input = 2000 × 210 = 420 000 J, efficiency = 336 000 ÷ 420 000 = 0.80 (80%); Kettle B: t = 180 s, input = 2400 × 180 = 432 000 J, efficiency = 336 000 ÷ 432 000 = 0.78 (78%); kettle A is more efficient (although B is faster).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both efficiencies correct with units converted and the correct kettle identified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one input energy or one efficiency correct.
questions.explanation: Convert minutes to seconds and kW to W, find each input with E = P × t, then divide the useful 336 000 J by each input. The faster kettle is not the more efficient one.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows an electric motor lifting a mass.
The input power to the motor is 40 W. The motor runs for 6.0 s and lifts a 2.0 kg mass through a height of 9.0 m.
Calculate the efficiency of the motor.
